## The Behavioral Health Crisis

160 million Americans live in mental health professional shortage areas. Demand for services has surged 40% since 2020, but the workforce has grown only 10%.

### The Supply Challenge

| Profession | Active Practitioners | Estimated Need | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Psychiatrists | 37,000 | 55,000 | -33% |
| Psychologists | 106,000 | 140,000 | -24% |
| LCSW | 250,000 | 320,000 | -22% |
| Counselors | 370,000 | 450,000 | -18% |

### Why Behavioral Health Professionals Leave

- Burnout (52%): Caseload overwhelm and emotional exhaustion
- Compensation (28%): Below-market pay relative to training required
- Administrative burden (15%): Insurance paperwork, EHR documentation
- Lack of support (5%): Insufficient supervision and peer consultation

### Attraction Strategies

Compensation Innovation :

- Loan repayment programs ($10K-$50K over 3-5 years)
- Competitive hourly rates for contractors ($80-$150/hour)
- Sign-on bonuses ($5K-$15K)

Work Model Flexibility :

- Telehealth-first positions (expand geographic reach)
- Hybrid schedules (2-3 days in-office)
- Reduced caseloads with sustainable workload policies

Career Development :

- Supervision hours for licensure (paid)
- Continuing education funding
- Specialized training opportunities
- Research and publication support

### Telehealth as a Hiring Multiplier

Telehealth-enabled positions:

- Expand the talent pool geographically
- Reduce commute-related attrition
- Allow flexible scheduling
- Enable multi-state practice (with appropriate licensure)

### Building the Pipeline

Long-term workforce development:

- Graduate program partnerships with stipend sponsorship
- Pre-licensure training positions with guaranteed employment
- Community health worker programs as entry pathways
- School counselor-to-clinical pipeline programs
